title: Stimulation and Training for Adaptive Balance and Locomotor Enhancement in Multiple Sclerosis
summary:
People with multiple sclerosis often experience problems with balance and walking, which can affect their daily life and increase the risk of falling. In addition, these physical difficulties can also influence mental well-being.

The aim of this study is to investigate whether combining a gentle brain stimulation technique with balance training can improve balance, walking ability, and overall well-being in people with multiple sclerosis.

Participants will take part in a 3-week training program with three sessions per week. Before each training session, they will receive a mild and painless electrical stimulation through small electrodes placed on the head. Another group will receive a similar procedure without active stimulation. All participants will also receive their usual rehabilitation program at the clinic.

We will assess balance, walking ability, and well-being before and after the program, as well as during a follow-up period over several months.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (according to established clinical criteria); Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) ≤ 6.0; no relapse within the last 3 months; ability to stand and walk independently (with or without assistive devices); indication for balance training as determined by clinical assessment; ability to understand study procedures and provide written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
Severe cognitive impairment preventing understanding of instructions; other neurological or musculoskeletal disorders affecting balance or gait; acute relapse of multiple sclerosis within the last 3 months; contraindications to transcranial direct current stimulation (e.g., implanted electronic devices, active skin lesions at electrode sites); severe comorbid medical conditions limiting participation; pregnancy.
